Title: Cancer Overview
Source:
- https://cancerprogressreport.aacr.org/progress/cpr25-contents/cpr25-understanding-the-path-to-cancer-development/
- https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/01/260125083344.htm
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10618731/
- https://edition.cnn.com/

- https://www.bbc.com/
- https://www.who.int/
- https://www.bloomberg.com/latest
- https://www.euronews.com/
Last Updated: 2024–2026

---

Overview
- Cancer is a group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow uncontrollably. - These cells can invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymph system. - The spread of cancer to distant organs is called metastasis, and it is a major cause of cancer-related death. How cancer develops
- Cancer often starts with changes in a cell's DNA. - DNA changes can happen because of errors during cell division, harmful exposures such as tobacco smoke or radiation, inherited mutations, infections, and environmental or lifestyle factors. - As abnormal cells continue to divide, they may form tumors and spread through the bloodstream or lymphatic system. Common types
- There are more than 100 types of cancer. - Carcinoma begins in epithelial cells and includes lung, breast, and colorectal cancer. - Sarcoma develops in bones, muscles, fat, or connective tissues. - Leukemia affects blood-forming tissues such as the bone marrow and blood cells. - Lymphoma affects the lymphatic system and immune cells. - Melanoma develops in pigment-producing cells called melanocytes. Cancer statistics
- In 2022, there were about 20 million new cancer cases and 9.7 million cancer deaths worldwide. - Lung cancer was the most commonly diagnosed cancer in 2022 and the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. - Other common cancers include breast, colorectal, prostate, and stomach cancer. - Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide. - About 400,000 children develop cancer each year worldwide. Main risk factors
- Cancer risk factors increase the chance of developing cancer, but they do not guarantee that a person will get cancer.

1.content:
breast, colorectal, prostate, and stomach cancer. - Cancer remains one of the leading causes of death worldwide. - About 400,000 children develop cancer each year worldwide. Main risk factors - Cancer risk factors increase the chance of developing cancer, but they do not guarantee that a person will get cancer. - Risk rises with age. - Tobacco use strongly increases cancer risk. - Heavy alcohol use raises the risk of several cancers. - Family history and inherited gene changes can increase risk. - Excess body weight and low physical activity increase the risk of several cancers. - UV exposure from sunlight or tanning beds increases skin cancer risk. - Infections such as HPV can increase cancer risk. - Environmental exposures such as radon, asbestos, secondhand smoke, and certain chemicals can raise risk. Prevention strategies
- Avoid tobacco and secondhand smoke. - Maintain a healthy weight. - Be physically active. - Eat a healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and beans. - Limit alcohol. - Protect yourself from the sun. - Get vaccinated against HPV and hepatitis B when appropriate. - Use screening tests such as mammograms, Pap tests, colonoscopy, and low-dose CT when recommended.

Title: Cancer Staging and Classification
Source:
- https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553187/
- https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/22607-cancer-stages-grades-system
- https://www.worldwidecancerresearch.org/cancer-and-research-information/diagnosis-prevention-and-treatment/cancer-stages-and-grades-explained-what-they-mean-and-why-they-matter/
- https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diagnostics/22607-cancer-stages-grades-system
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5215238/
- https://www.mdanderson.org/patients-family/diagnosis-treatment/a-new-diagnosis/cancer-grade-vs--cancer-stage.html
- https://www.worldwidecancerresearch.org/cancer-and-research-information/diagnosis-prevention-and-treatment/cancer-stages-and-grades-explained-what-they-mean-and-why-they-matter/
- https://www.foxchase.org/blog/cancer-staging-why-its-important-and-why-accuracy-matters
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5215238/

Last Updated:  January 1, 2026

---

TNM staging system
- TNM is a standard system for describing how far a cancer has spread. - T means the size and extent of the primary tumor. - N means whether nearby lymph nodes contain cancer. - M means whether the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. - TX means the primary tumor cannot be assessed. - T0 means there is no evidence of a primary tumor. - Tis means carcinoma in situ, which is early cancer limited to the original cell layer. - T1 through T4 mean increasing size or local spread of the tumor. - NX means nearby lymph nodes cannot be assessed. - N0 means no cancer is found in nearby lymph nodes. - N1 through N3 mean increasing spread to nearby lymph nodes. - M0 means no distant metastasis is detected. - M1 means the cancer has spread to distant organs or tissues. - TNM is often written as a combination such as T2N1M0. - In that example, the tumor is moderately sized, there is lymph node involvement, and there is no distant metastasis. - TNM is especially used for solid tumors. Stage 0 to stage 4
- Stage 0 is also called carcinoma in situ. - Stage 0 means abnormal cells are present but have not spread into nearby tissue. - Stage 1 means the cancer is small and confined to the original site. - Stage 1 usually means there is little or no spread to nearby lymph nodes.

3.content:
is also called carcinoma in situ. - Stage 0 means abnormal cells are present but have not spread into nearby tissue. - Stage 1 means the cancer is small and confined to the original site. - Stage 1 usually means there is little or no spread to nearby lymph nodes. - Stage 2 means the tumor is larger than stage 1 or has started to spread into nearby tissue or a small number of nearby lymph nodes. - Stage 3 means the cancer has grown deeper into nearby tissues and may involve more nearby lymph nodes, but it has not spread to distant organs. - Stage 4 means the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. - Stage 4 is also called metastatic cancer. - Stage 4 cancer can spread to organs such as the lungs, liver, bones, or brain. How staging affects treatment
- Stage 0 and stage 1 cancers are often treated with local treatments such as surgery, radiation, or both. - Stage 2 and stage 3 cancers often need a combination of treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy. - Stage 4 cancers usually need systemic therapy such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy. - Staging also helps doctors estimate prognosis, plan follow-up, and decide whether the goal is cure, long-term control, or symptom relief. Grading vs staging
- Staging describes how much cancer is in the body and where it has spread. - Grading describes how abnormal the cancer cells look under the microscope. - Lower-grade cancers look more like normal cells. - Higher-grade cancers look more abnormal and are often more aggressive. Why accurate staging matters
- Accurate staging helps doctors choose the right treatment. - Under-staging can lead to treatment that is too weak.

Title: Cancer Symptoms
Source:
- https://www.cancer.org/cancer/diagnosis-staging/signs-and-symptoms-of-cancer.html
- https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/wellness-and-prevention/early-cancer-warning-signs-5-symptoms-you-shouldnt-ignore
- https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/cancer/symptoms-causes/syc-20370588
- https://www.bangkokhospital.com/en/bangkok-cancer/content/the-importance-of-early-detection-of-cancer
- https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/spot-cancer-early/why-is-early-diagnosis-important
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6941215/
- https://www.ucsfhealth.org/health-articles/17-cancer-symptoms-you-shouldnt-ignore
Last Updated: 2026

---

General warning signs
- Unexplained weight loss or weight change can be a warning sign. - Fatigue that does not improve with rest can be concerning. - A new lump or swelling should be checked. - Unusual bleeding or discharge can be a warning sign. - A sore that does not heal needs evaluation. - Changes in bowel or bladder habits can matter. - Persistent cough, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing should not be ignored. - Skin changes, including a changing mole or new skin lesion, can be important. - These symptoms do not always mean cancer. - The key concern is whether the symptom is new, persistent, or getting worse. Common symptoms by cancer type
- Lung cancer may cause persistent cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, frequent lung infections, or hoarseness. - Breast cancer may cause a lump in the breast or underarm, changes in breast shape or size, nipple discharge, or skin dimpling and redness. - Colorectal cancer may cause blood in stool, persistent diarrhea or constipation, abdominal pain or bloating, unexplained weight loss, or changes in bowel habits. - Prostate cancer may cause difficulty urinating, frequent urination, blood in urine or semen, pelvic discomfort, a weak urine stream, trouble starting urination, or pain when urinating. - Skin cancer may cause new or changing moles, irregular borders, uneven color, sores that do not heal, or unusual skin color changes. - Cervical or endometrial cancer may cause abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, pain during intercourse, unusual vaginal discharge, or bleeding after menopause. - Ovarian cancer may cause bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full quickly, appetite changes, or urinary changes.

6.content:
sores that do not heal, or unusual skin color changes. - Cervical or endometrial cancer may cause abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, pain during intercourse, unusual vaginal discharge, or bleeding after menopause. - Ovarian cancer may cause bloating, pelvic or abdominal pain, feeling full quickly, appetite changes, or urinary changes. - Pancreatic cancer may cause upper abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, poor appetite, new diabetes, or jaundice. - Liver cancer may cause jaundice, abdominal swelling or pain, loss of appetite, fatigue, or weakness. - Stomach cancer may cause persistent indigestion, loss of appetite, stomach pain, nausea or vomiting, or feeling full quickly after eating. - Lymphoma or leukemia may cause swollen lymph nodes, fever, night sweats, fatigue, frequent infections, easy bruising, or unexplained weight loss. Early detection importance
- Early detection matters because cancer found sooner is usually smaller and easier to treat. - Treatment is often more effective when cancer is still at an early stage. - Early treatment can offer more options, including local treatment such as surgery. - Early detection can reduce treatment intensity, side effects, and long-term complications. - Early detection can improve survival and quality of life. - Screening can find some cancers before symptoms appear. - New symptoms should also be checked early because some cancers do not cause obvious symptoms until they are advanced. When to seek medical attention
- Seek medical attention for a new lump or swelling. - Seek medical attention for unexplained weight loss. - Seek medical attention for persistent cough, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing. - Seek medical attention for unusual bleeding or discharge. - Seek medical attention for a sore that does not heal. - Seek medical attention for changes in bowel or bladder habits. - Seek medical attention for ongoing pain without a clear cause.

Symptom variations by stage
- Early stage cancers may cause no symptoms or only subtle local signs. - Middle stage cancers are more likely to cause pain, swelling, cough, hoarseness, trouble swallowing, or enlarged lymph nodes. - Advanced stage cancers are more likely to cause fatigue, weight loss, poor appetite, persistent pain, and symptoms from distant spread such as shortness of breath, jaundice, bone pain, headaches, or seizures.

Title: Cancer Treatment Options
Source:
- https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/types/surgery
- https://www.cancer.org/cancer/managing-cancer/treatment-types/surgery.html
- https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/16859-chemotherapy
- https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/chemotherapy/how-chemotherapy-works
- https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/types/radiation-therapy
- https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/17637-radiation-therapy
- https://www.cancerresearch.org/immunotherapy-by-cancer-type?campaign=784691
- https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/11582-immunotherapy
- https://www.bumrungrad.com/en/treatments/targeted-therapy
- https://www.cancer.org/cancer/managing-cancer/treatment-types/targeted-therapy.html
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5514969/
- https://www.msdmanuals.com/home/cancer/prevention-and-treatment-of-cancer/combination-cancer-therapy
Last Updated: 2026

---

Surgery
- Surgery can remove the whole tumor, remove part of a tumor to reduce symptoms, or take tissue for diagnosis and staging. - Surgery is a local treatment and works best for solid tumors in one area. - Curative surgery aims to remove all visible cancer. - Debulking surgery removes as much cancer as possible when full removal is not possible. - Palliative surgery helps relieve pain, pressure, bleeding, or blockage. - Diagnostic or staging surgery helps confirm cancer and see how far it has spread. - Surgery is often combined with chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy. - Surgery is usually not enough by itself for cancers that have spread widely. Chemotherapy
- Chemotherapy uses drugs to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing and dividing. - It targets rapidly dividing cells and can shrink tumors or slow cancer spread. - Chemotherapy may be given before surgery, after surgery, together with radiation, or to control cancer that has spread. - Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, fatigue, mouth sores, hair loss, low blood counts, infection risk, constipation or diarrhea, and nerve tingling. - If a tumor is too large for surgery at first, chemotherapy may be used first to make it smaller. Radiation therapy
- Radiation therapy uses high-energy radiation, usually X-rays, to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing. - It damages the DNA of cancer cells so they can no longer divide normally. - Radiation may be the main treatment, or it may be used before surgery, after surgery, together with chemotherapy, or to relieve symptoms.

9.content:
radiation, usually X-rays, to kill cancer cells or stop them from growing. - It damages the DNA of cancer cells so they can no longer divide normally. - Radiation may be the main treatment, or it may be used before surgery, after surgery, together with chemotherapy, or to relieve symptoms. - External beam radiation comes from a machine outside the body. - Internal radiation therapy, also called brachytherapy, places radioactive material inside or near the tumor. - Common side effects depend on the treatment area and may include skin irritation, tiredness, appetite loss, nausea, and local tissue inflammation. Immunotherapy
- Immunotherapy helps the body’s immune system recognize and attack cancer cells. - It can boost immune activity, remove the brakes on immune cells, or give the immune system agents that help it attack cancer more effectively. - Main types include checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T or T-cell therapy, monoclonal antibodies, and cancer vaccines. - Immunotherapy is often used for cancers that have spread, come back, or do not respond well to other treatments. - Side effects can include fatigue, skin changes, flu-like symptoms, and inflammation in organs such as the lungs, liver, intestines, or thyroid. Targeted therapy
- Targeted therapy uses drugs to attack specific molecules, genes, or proteins that help cancer cells grow and spread. - It is designed to hit a more specific cancer feature than standard chemotherapy. - Targeted therapy may block growth signals, stop tumor cells from dividing, or cut off blood vessel growth. - It is often used when the cancer has a known biomarker or mutation. - Main types include monoclonal antibodies and small-molecule drugs. - Common side effects include skin problems, diarrhea, and high blood pressure. - Not every cancer has a targetable mutation, and some cancers can develop resistance over time.

10.content:
It is often used when the cancer has a known biomarker or mutation. - Main types include monoclonal antibodies and small-molecule drugs. - Common side effects include skin problems, diarrhea, and high blood pressure. - Not every cancer has a targetable mutation, and some cancers can develop resistance over time. Combination treatments
- Combination treatments use two or more cancer therapies together. - Combining treatments can improve effectiveness, reduce resistance, and treat both local and spread disease. - Neoadjuvant therapy is given before surgery to shrink a tumor. - Adjuvant therapy is given after surgery to kill any remaining cancer cells. - Concurrent therapy gives treatments at the same time, such as chemotherapy with radiation. - Combination treatment can be more effective, but it may also cause more side effects. Clinical trials
- Clinical trials are research studies in people that test new ways to prevent, detect, diagnose, or treat cancer. - They help determine whether a new treatment is safe and effective. - Main types include treatment trials, prevention trials, screening or diagnostic trials, and supportive care trials. - Trial phases usually move from safety and dose testing to efficacy testing and then comparison with standard care. - Clinical trials are not only for people with no other options.

Title: Diabetes Complications
Source: 
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5866895/
- https://idf.org/about-diabetes/complications/

Last Updated: 2026

---

Short-term Complications
- Short-term complications of diabetes can happen suddenly and may become serious if not treated quickly. - These include hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, and diabetic ketoacidosis. - Symptoms may include dizziness, confusion, thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue. - Proper monitoring of blood glucose levels can help prevent these complications. Long-term Complications
- Long-term complications develop gradually when blood sugar levels remain uncontrolled for a long period. - Diabetes can damage blood vessels and organs, leading to heart disease, kidney disease, nerve damage, and eye problems. - Maintaining healthy blood sugar levels can reduce the risk of these conditions. Heart Disease and Diabetes
- People with diabetes are more likely to develop cardiovascular diseases such as heart attack and stroke. - High blood sugar can damage blood vessels and increase blood pressure and cholesterol levels. - Regular exercise, healthy eating, and medication can help lower the risk of heart disease. Kidney Disease
- Diabetes is one of the leading causes of kidney disease. - High blood sugar damages the small blood vessels in the kidneys, reducing their ability to filter waste from the blood. - Early signs may include swelling, fatigue, and changes in urination. - Regular kidney function tests are important for people with diabetes. Neuropathy
- Diabetic neuropathy is nerve damage caused by prolonged high blood sugar levels. - It often affects the feet and hands, causing numbness, tingling, pain, or weakness. - Proper foot care and blood sugar control can help prevent severe nerve damage.

12.content:
Title: Diabetes Management
Source: 
- https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/diabetes/overview/managing-diabetes
- https://www.who.int/southeastasia/activities/management-of-diabetes

Last Updated: 2026

---

Blood Sugar Monitoring
- Blood sugar monitoring is important because it helps track whether blood glucose levels are within a healthy range. - Patients can use finger-prick glucose meters or continuous glucose monitoring devices. - Regular monitoring helps prevent complications and allows doctors to adjust treatment plans effectively. Insulin Therapy
- Insulin therapy is an essential treatment for some people with diabetes, especially those with Type 1 diabetes. - Insulin helps control blood sugar levels and keeps them within a normal range. - Insulin is available in different forms such as injections and insulin pens. - Patients should use insulin according to their doctor’s instructions. Oral Medications
- Oral medications for diabetes help lower blood sugar levels and improve the body’s ability to use insulin. - Doctors prescribe different medications depending on the patient’s condition. - Taking medications regularly and correctly is important for effective diabetes management. Diet and Nutrition
- Healthy eating plays a major role in diabetes management. - People with diabetes should reduce sugary foods, high-fat foods, and processed foods while increasing vegetables, fruits, and whole grains. - Maintaining balanced meals and controlling portion sizes can help regulate blood sugar levels. Exercise Recommendations
- Regular exercise helps control blood sugar levels and improves insulin sensitivity. - Recommended activities include walking, jogging, cycling, and swimming. - People with diabetes should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week. Regular Check-ups
- Regular medical check-ups help monitor diabetes and prevent complications. - Patients should routinely check blood sugar levels, blood pressure, kidney function, and eye health. - Visiting healthcare professionals regularly allows for better treatment adjustments and overall health management.

13.content:
Title: Diabetes Overview
Source:
- https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/diabetes
- https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/about/index.html

Last Updated: 2026

---

Definition of Diabetes
- Diabetes is a chronic disease that occurs when the body cannot properly regulate blood sugar levels. - This happens when the body does not produce enough insulin or cannot effectively use the insulin it produces. - High blood sugar levels over time can lead to serious health complications affecting many parts of the body. Type 1 vs Type 2 Differences
- Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. - People with Type 1 diabetes usually require insulin therapy for life. - Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body becomes resistant to insulin or does not produce enough insulin. - Type 2 diabetes is more common and is often linked to lifestyle factors such as obesity and lack of physical activity. Risk Factors
- Family history can increase the risk of developing diabetes. - Obesity, unhealthy diet, and physical inactivity are common risk factors. - High blood pressure and age can also increase risk. - For Type 1 diabetes, genetics and autoimmune factors may play an important role. Statistics and Prevalence
- Diabetes affects millions of people worldwide and continues to increase each year. - Type 2 diabetes accounts for the majority of diabetes cases. - The growing prevalence of diabetes is associated with changes in lifestyle, aging populations, and increasing obesity rates. Impact on the Body
- Diabetes can affect many organs and systems in the body. - High blood sugar levels may damage blood vessels, nerves, kidneys, eyes, and the heart. - If not properly managed, diabetes can lead to cardiovascular disease, kidney failure, nerve damage, and vision problems.

Title: Diabetes Symptoms
Source:
- https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/diabetes/symptoms-causes/syc-20371444
- https://www.bangkokhospital.com/en/pattaya/content/diabetes-symptoms-risk-bph
Last Updated: 2026

---

Early Warning Signs
- Early warning signs of diabetes may include increased thirst, frequent urination, unusual hunger, fatigue, blurred vision, and unexplained weight loss. - Some people may also experience slow-healing wounds or frequent infections. - Recognizing these signs early can help prevent serious complications. Common Symptoms for Type 1
- Type 1 diabetes symptoms usually develop quickly, often within a few weeks. - Common symptoms include extreme thirst, frequent urination, sudden weight loss, fatigue, and increased hunger. - Some patients may also experience nausea or diabetic ketoacidosis, which requires immediate medical attention. Common Symptoms for Type 2
- Type 2 diabetes symptoms often develop slowly and may go unnoticed for years. - Common symptoms include tiredness, blurred vision, increased thirst, frequent urination, slow-healing cuts, and numbness in the hands or feet. - Many people discover they have Type 2 diabetes during routine health check-ups. Symptoms in Children
- Children with diabetes may experience excessive thirst, frequent urination, bed-wetting, tiredness, irritability, and weight loss. - Parents should seek medical attention if these symptoms appear suddenly or become severe. When Symptoms Appear
- Symptoms of Type 1 diabetes usually appear suddenly. - Symptoms of Type 2 diabetes develop gradually over time. - Some individuals may not notice any symptoms until complications begin to occur.

Title: Migraine Overview

Definition of Migraine
- Migraine is a neurological disorder characterized by recurring attacks of moderate to severe headaches. - The pain is often throbbing or pulsating and commonly affects one side of the head. - Migraine attacks can last from several hours to several days. - Symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light, sound, or smells. - Some people experience aura before the headache begins. Types of Migraine
- Migraine without aura is the most common type and does not include warning signs. - Migraine with aura includes temporary neurological symptoms such as flashes of light, blind spots, tingling, or speech difficulties. - Chronic migraine occurs on 15 or more days per month for at least three months. - Menstrual migraine is linked to hormonal changes during the menstrual cycle. - Hemiplegic migraine can cause temporary weakness on one side of the body. - Retinal migraine causes temporary visual disturbances or vision loss in one eye. - Abdominal migraine is more common in children and causes abdominal pain with migraine-related symptoms. - Silent migraine includes aura symptoms without a significant headache. Prevalence and Statistics
- Migraine is one of the most common neurological disorders worldwide. - The World Health Organization reports that headache disorders affect about 40% of the global population, with migraine a major contributor to disability. - Migraine is more common in females than males. - It often begins during puberty or early adulthood. - Around 12% of people in the United States experience migraines. - Migraine is a leading cause of disability-adjusted life years globally. Key Characteristics
- Moderate to severe throbbing or pulsating head pain. - Pain often on one side of the head. - Sensitivity to light and sound. - Nausea and vomiting.

Title: Migraine Symptoms
Source: Migraine.txt
Last Updated: 2026

---

Early Warning Signs (Prodrome)
- The prodrome phase may begin several hours or up to two days before the headache starts. - Common signs include mood changes, fatigue, food cravings, neck stiffness, increased thirst, frequent urination, constipation, difficulty concentrating, and excessive yawning. - Recognizing prodrome symptoms may help a person prepare for or manage an upcoming migraine attack. Aura Symptoms
- Aura symptoms occur in some people before or during a migraine attack. - They usually develop gradually over several minutes and last 5 to 60 minutes. - Common visual symptoms include flashing lights, blind spots, zigzag patterns, and blurred vision. - Other aura symptoms may include numbness or tingling in the face, arms, or legs, weakness, dizziness, ringing in the ears, and difficulty speaking or concentrating. - Aura symptoms are temporary and reversible. Headache Phase Symptoms
- Migraine pain is typically throbbing or pulsating and often affects one side of the head. - The headache may worsen with physical activity. - Common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light, sound, smells, or touch. - Some people also experience dizziness, blurred vision, or extreme fatigue. - The severity can significantly interfere with daily activities and quality of life. Post-Headache Phase (Postdrome)
- The postdrome stage is often called a migraine hangover. - It may last from several hours to up to 48 hours. - Common symptoms include fatigue, weakness, dizziness, difficulty concentrating, body aches, mood changes, and continued sensitivity to light and sound. - Some people feel mentally drained or confused, while others may feel temporary relief or mild euphoria. Typical Symptom Duration
- Prodrome symptoms may begin 24 to 48 hours before the headache. - Aura symptoms generally last between 5 and 60 minutes.

changes, and continued sensitivity to light and sound. - Some people feel mentally drained or confused, while others may feel temporary relief or mild euphoria. Typical Symptom Duration - Prodrome symptoms may begin 24 to 48 hours before the headache. - Aura symptoms generally last between 5 and 60 minutes. - The headache phase commonly lasts from 4 to 72 hours if untreated. - The postdrome phase can continue for several hours or up to two days. - A full migraine attack may span several days from beginning to recovery. Symptom Triggers
- Common triggers include emotional stress, hormonal changes, lack of sleep, oversleeping, dehydration, skipped meals, and intense physical activity. - Environmental triggers may include bright lights, loud noises, strong smells, and weather changes. - Food and beverage triggers can include alcohol, caffeine, chocolate, aged cheese, processed foods, and additives such as monosodium glutamate. - Identifying personal triggers may help reduce the frequency of migraine attacks.

Title: Migraine Treatment
Source: Migraine.txt
Last Updated: 2026

---

Over-the-counter Medications
- Over-the-counter medications are commonly used to relieve mild to moderate migraine symptoms. - Common examples include acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and aspirin. - These medications may help reduce pain and discomfort when taken early during a migraine attack. Prescription Medications
- Prescription medications are often recommended for severe or frequent migraines. - Doctors may prescribe triptans, anti-nausea medications, or other migraine-specific drugs. - These medicines can help reduce symptoms and improve daily functioning. Acute Treatment Strategies
- Acute treatment focuses on stopping symptoms after they begin. - People are often advised to rest in a quiet, dark room, stay hydrated, and take medication as soon as symptoms appear. - Early treatment may reduce the severity and duration of attacks. Prevention Medications
- Preventive medications are used to reduce the frequency and intensity of migraine attacks. - Examples include blood pressure medications, antidepressants, anti-seizure drugs, and CGRP inhibitors. - Preventive treatment is usually considered for people who have frequent migraines. Non-drug Therapies
- Non-drug therapies can help manage migraines and improve quality of life. - Common approaches include relaxation techniques, acupuncture, massage therapy, biofeedback, and cognitive behavioral therapy. - These methods may help reduce stress and migraine triggers. Lifestyle Modifications
- Healthy lifestyle habits can help prevent migraines. - Important habits include getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, eating balanced meals, drinking enough water, and avoiding known triggers such as stress, alcohol, or certain foods. - Keeping a migraine diary may help identify triggers and patterns.

20.content:
Title: When to See a Doctor for Migraine
Source: Migraine.txt
Last Updated: 2026

---

Red Flags and Warning Signs
- Sudden severe headaches should be checked. - Headaches after a head injury need medical attention. - Vision problems, confusion, difficulty speaking, weakness, or numbness are warning signs. - Headaches with fever and a stiff neck should not be ignored. When to Seek Emergency Care
- Emergency care should be sought if a headache is extremely sudden and severe, sometimes described as the worst headache of your life. - Seek emergency help if migraines are associated with seizures, loss of consciousness, chest pain, or stroke-like symptoms such as facial drooping or difficulty moving parts of the body. Recommended Specialist (Neurologist)
- People with frequent, severe, or unusual migraines may benefit from seeing a neurologist. - A neurologist can help diagnose migraine types, recommend treatments, and rule out other neurological conditions. Importance of Medical Consultation
- Medical consultation is important because migraines can significantly affect daily life. - Migraines may sometimes be confused with other serious health conditions. - A doctor can provide diagnosis, personalized treatment plans, and recommendations to reduce frequency and severity. Headache Diary Recommendation
- Keeping a headache diary can help identify migraine triggers and patterns. - Useful details include when migraines occur, symptoms, food intake, stress levels, medications used, and possible triggers. - This information can improve migraine management and treatment decisions.
